power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > .999", Text = "Follow-up comparisons revealed that younger adults showed greater synchrony with other younger adults than with older adults (t(28) = 5.98, p < .001 corrected, Cohen's d = 0.47, 95% CI [0.34, 0.67]), whereas older adults showed comparable synchrony with individuals in either age group (t(23) = 0.59, p > .999 corrected, Cohen's d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.23])."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

live_data_statements: Twenty-nine younger and twenty-four older adult participants were presented with a "sliceof-life" television sitcom (HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm) while undergoing functional MRI scanning (Fig. 1A).
After viewing, participants were instructed to recall aloud everything that they can remember about the television episode in as much detail as possible (Fig. 1B).
However, ISPS was associated with reinstatement even when participants were compared with others in their own age group.
Sixty-five participants were initially recruited (39 younger adults and 26 older adults).
All fifty-three participants were included in encoding analyses (ISC and ISPS).
Participants were presented with a fixation cross in the center of a computer screen and were instructed to verbally recall everything that they can remember about the episode (Fig. 1B).
Participants were encouraged to continue recalling for as long as they remembered additional details.

Four older adults scored below the conventional MoCA cutoff of 26 (three of whom were included in recall analyses); however, given that the MoCA is a screening instrument rather than a diagnostic measure, these participants were retained in all analyses.
All main results remained when these participants were excluded (Tables S5 and S6).
Participants were briefed on the experiment and provided written informed consent.
Upon successful screening for the experiment, participants were escorted to the Imaging Research Center and were prepared to undergo scanning.
Participants were provided MRI-compatible earbuds with replaceable foam inserts (MRIaudio) as well as additional foam padding inside the head coil for hearing protection and to mitigate head motion.
Participants were also given bodily padding, blankets, and corrective lenses as needed.
Participants were given a description of strategies to remain still while speaking during functional image acquisition.
While in the fMRI scanner, participants were presented with an episode of a television sitcom (HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm, S01E07: AAMCO).
Participants were then instructed to recall the episode in as much detail as possible during fMRI scanning.
Participants were recruited from the University of California, Davis and the Davis, California community through online advertisement, flyers, and word of mouth.

Participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, Davis, Project Title: Naturalistic Memory and Neurocognitive Aging (ID #: 1198619) protocol, and were compensated $20 per hour.

text.text: Remembering an experience can reinstate patterns of neural activity from when the event originally occurred.
During encoding, individuals show synchronized neural responses as events unfold, and greater synchrony across individuals has been linked to better memory.
These shared neural responses may reflect aspects of an event that are consistently represented and could support later reinstatement.
Yet whether greater similarity to others is associated with stronger reinstatement remains unclear, particularly in older adults, whose neural responses are more variable.
Here, younger and older adults watched a 26-minute television episode and then freely recalled it while in the scanner.
We measured moment-to-moment neural synchrony and eventspecific spatial similarity across individuals in the posterior medial network (PMN).
We then examined how these measures related to neural reinstatement and recall specificity.
Older adults recalled fewer specific details and showed less similar event-specific encoding patterns to one another compared to younger adults.
However, their patterns were more similar to those of younger adults than to those of other older adults.
Both groups showed event-specific reinstatement.
Importantly, individuals whose encoding patterns more closely resembled those of other viewers showed stronger reinstatement in both age groups.
Greater neural synchrony was also associated with more specific recall in younger adults, although this relationship did not differ significantly between age groups.

Together, these findings establish a link between how similarly experiences are represented across individuals during encoding and how strongly those representations are reinstated during remembering, even in the context of greater neural variability in older adulthood.

Remembering everyday experiences involves reconstructing meaningful events that bring together information about people, places, and actions encoded during the original experience (Radvansky & Zacks, 2014; Zacks, 2020; Reagh & Ranganath, 2023).

text.text: Among the corticohippocampal networks that support episodic memory (Ranganath & Ritchey, 2012), the posterior medial network (PMN), consisting of the posterior cingulate cortex, retrosplenial cortex, angular gyrus, and dorsal prefrontal cortex (Barnett et al., 2021), has been implicated in representing the structure of events and maintaining event models that integrate information over extended timescales (Zacks, 2020; Baldassano et al., 2017; Ritchey & Cooper, 2020).

text.text: Although reinstatement is generally measured within individuals, the neural representations formed during experience are not entirely unique to each individual.

When different individuals experience the same continuous events, they exhibit similar spatial patterns of activity in the PMN and other higher-order cortical regions (Chen et al., 2017; Oedekoven et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017).

text.text: These findings suggest that both the spatial organization and moment-tomoment temporal dynamics of shared neural responses during encoding may be relevant to later remembering.

However, these relationships with memory performance do not address the question of whether similarity across individuals during encoding is also related to the reinstatement of an individual's own neural representations.
For instance, an individual could encode an event differently from others yet still strongly reinstate their own encoding pattern during recall.

Alternatively, if shared neural patterns reflect common representations of event content and structure, individuals whose encoding patterns more closely resemble those of others may show stronger reinstatement.

Greater similarity across individuals could also reflect more consistent processing of the unfolding experience or more reliable encoding representations, which may contribute to stronger reinstatement.

Although these possibilities are not mutually exclusive, they SHARED EVENT REPRESENTATION IN PMN PREDICTS REINSTATEMENT 5 raise an important question about whether the extent to which neural representations are shared across individuals during encoding is associated with how strongly individuals reinstate those representations during remembering.

Examining this relationship would extend previous findings linking shared neural responses to behavioral memory by identifying whether they are also related to the neural reactivation of past experiences.
Aging provides an important context for examining this relationship as older adults show changes in episodic memory and in the neural processes supporting event representations.

Older adults often retain the general meaning of past experiences while recalling fewer specific details (Grilli & Sheldon, 2022; Greene & Naveh-Benjamin, 2023), and they tend to organize their recall of naturalistic events around broader topics rather than the fine-grained temporal sequence that characterizes younger adults' recall (Delarazan et al., 2026).

text.text: These findings suggest that aging may affect the consistency with which individuals represent the same events.

However, it is poorly understood whether older adults' less consistent neural responses reflect a shift toward distinct age-specific event representations or greater individual variability in representations that remain shared across age groups.
It is also unclear whether older adults whose encoding patterns more closely resemble those of others show stronger reinstatement, despite greater variability in their neural responses.
Here, we examined whether shared neural representations during encoding were associated with later memory and event-specific reinstatement in younger and older adults.
During functional MRI scanning (fMRI), participants watched a 26-minute episode of a "slice-of-life" television sitcom (HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm) and provided an unconstrained spoken recall.

Focusing on the PMN, we measured shared neural responses during encoding using intersubject correlation (ISC) to assess moment-to-moment neural synchrony and intersubject pattern similarity (ISPS) to assess event-specific spatial similarity.
We compared neural responses within and across age groups and examined how these measures related to later reinstatement and behavioral recall specificity.
We found that older adults recalled the episode with fewer specific details and that their event-specific encoding patterns were less similar to one another than those of younger adults.

Interestingly, older adults' encoding patterns were more similar to those of younger adults than to those of other older adults, and event-specific reinstatement was evident in both age groups, although it was weaker in older adults.
Individuals whose event-specific encoding patterns were more similar to those of others showed stronger reinstatement in both younger and older adults.
Neural synchrony during encoding was also associated with more specific recall in younger adults.

Together, these findings suggest that shared event-specific representations during encoding are related to reinstatement in both younger and older adults, despite age-related differences in the consistency of these representations across individuals.

We correlated recall specificity with within-group and cross-group ISC and ISPS, as well as pattern reinstatement, separately for each age group.

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that greater moment-to-moment neural synchrony during encoding was associated with more specific recall in younger adults but not older adults, although this association did not differ significantly between age groups.
The present study examined whether shared neural representations of naturalistic events during encoding were associated with reinstatement and recall specificity in younger and older adults.

We found that individuals whose event-specific encoding patterns in the posterior medial network (PMN) more closely resembled those of others showed stronger reinstatement during recall in both age groups.
Older adults recalled the episode with lower specificity and showed weaker event-specific reinstatement than younger adults.
They also showed greater variability in event-specific encoding patterns, and their patterns were more similar to those of younger adults than to one another.
Greater neural synchrony during encoding was associated with more specific recall in younger adults, although this relationship did not differ significantly between age groups.

By linking shared neural representations during encoding to their reinstatement within individuals, this study connects how experiences are represented across people with how they are reactivated during remembering.

Prior work has shown that individuals exhibit shared neural representations when experiencing the same naturalistic events (Chen et al., 2017; Oedekoven et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017), and that greater similarity in neural responses across individuals during encoding is associated with better memory (Koch et al., 2020; Sheng et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Prior work has shown that individuals exhibit shared neural representations when experiencing the same naturalistic events <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Oedekoven et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zadbood et al., 2017)</ref>, and that greater similarity in neural responses across individuals during encoding is associated with better memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Koch et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Sheng et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this work to reinstatement within individuals.
An individual could encode an event differently from others yet still reinstate that representation during recall.
However, we found that individuals whose encoding patterns were more similar to those of others showed stronger reinstatement.
One possibility is that greater similarity across individuals reflects common representations of event content and structure, possibly converging on central or important pieces of content.

The PMN is thought to integrate information about people, places, and actions over extended timescales, supporting coherent representations of unfolding events (Baldassano et al., 2017; Ritchey & Cooper, 2020; Reagh & Ranganath, 2023).
text.formatted: The PMN is thought to integrate information about people, places, and actions over extended timescales, supporting coherent representations of unfolding events <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baldassano et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ritchey & Cooper, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Reagh & Ranganath, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To the extent that individuals organize their experiences around similar event information, these representations may provide a framework for reconstructing those events during recall, potentially supporting stronger reinstatement of encoding patterns.

Alternatively, greater similarity across individuals may reflect more consistent processing of the unfolding experience or more reliable neural representations, both of which could increase similarity across individuals as well as between encoding and recall.

Although the present findings cannot distinguish among these explanations, they suggest that the extent to which an individual's encoding patterns resemble those of others may be relevant to why some individuals show stronger reinstatement than others.
Age-related differences in shared encoding patterns provide an important context for understanding this relationship.
Prior work has demonstrated that aging is associated with less synchronized and more idiosyncratic neural responses during naturalistic viewing (Campbell et al., 2015; Geerligs & Campbell, 2018).

text.text: The present findings extend this work by showing that greater variability among older adults is also evident in event-specific spatial representations within the PMN.

Interestingly, older adults' encoding patterns were more similar to those of younger adults than to other older adults, suggesting that aging may be associated with greater individual variability rather than a uniform shift toward distinct age-specific representations.
This raises the possibility that older adults retain aspects of shared event representations but differ in how they organize or emphasize information within those events.
For example, individuals may differ in the contextual information they attend to or integrate when constructing representations of unfolding experiences.

A similar pattern in early visual cortex (Table S3) suggests that this variability is not limited to higher-order event representations and may also reflect differences in SHARED EVENT REPRESENTATION IN PMN PREDICTS REINSTATEMENT 17 attention during encoding (Campbell et al., 2015).

text.text: Despite greater variability in their encoding patterns and weaker overall reinstatement, older adults whose event representations more closely resembled those of others showed stronger reinstatement.
Beyond the relationship between shared encoding patterns and reinstatement, we found that greater neural synchrony during encoding was associated with more specific recall among younger adults.
This finding extends prior work linking intersubject neural synchrony during naturalistic experiences to memory performance (Hasson et al., 2008; Simony et al., 2016; Cohen & Parra, 2016).

text.text: One possibility is that greater neural synchrony reflects more similar allocation of attention to the unfolding experience across individuals, consistent with prior work linking neural synchrony during naturalistic viewing to attentional control (Campbell et al., 2015).

text.text: Such attention may support the encoding of specific event information that can later be recalled.
Although this relationship was not significant among older adults, the associations did not differ significantly between age groups, limiting conclusions about age-related differences.

Nonetheless, it is possible that idiosyncratic processing of continuous events during encoding leads to relatively less stable event representations in older adults compared to younger adults, limiting the extent to which they can reinstate those representations during retrieval.
We also did not observe significant associations between recall specificity and either ISPS or pattern reinstatement.

First, our modest sample size, particularly among older adults with usable recall data, may have limited the precision of individual-difference estimates and our ability to detect age-related differences.
Nonetheless, the associations in older adults were relatively strong and remained when participants with lower neuropsychological scores were excluded (Tables S5 and S6).

text.text: Older adults' greater similarity to younger adults may also partly reflect the larger and more consistent younger adult group.
However, ISPS was associated with reinstatement even when participants were compared with others in their own age group.
Larger samples could provide more precise estimates of these relationships across adulthood.
Second, a key contribution of this study was linking shared eventspecific encoding patterns to reinstatement.
However, this association is correlational, and both measures relied on the same encoding patterns.
Individuals with more reliable PMN representations may therefore show greater similarity to others and stronger reinstatement.

We applied denoising and motion exclusion procedures, and the association was not observed in early visual cortex (Table S4), reducing concern about artifacts that affect neural similarity across regions.

text.text: However, these approaches cannot fully rule out differences in encoding reliability.
Future studies could independently assess encoding reliability or manipulate encoding conditions to better understand the factors contributing to this relationship.
Reinstatement was also measured only for successfully recalled events, leaving open whether shared encoding patterns relate to the likelihood of recalling particular events.
Finally, we focused on the PMN based on prior evidence of its role SHARED EVENT REPRESENTATION IN PMN PREDICTS REINSTATEMENT 19 in representing and reinstating naturalistic events.
Examining other neural systems and naturalistic experiences will be important for determining how broadly these relationships generalize across adulthood.
Together, our findings show that shared event-specific representations during encoding are associated with stronger reinstatement during recall.
This relationship was evident in both younger and older adults, despite greater variability in older adults' neural representations.

Although individuals may differ in how they represent the same experiences, the aspects of those representations that are shared across people may be important for understanding how events are later remembered.

Event Patterns.

To account for hemodynamic lag, timeseries were shifted by 5 TRs (6.1 s), and activity was averaged across all TRs corresponding to each event, yielding one spatial activity pattern per event in each hemisphere.
Only events that a participant successfully recalled were included in the reinstatement analyses.
These event-averaged encoding patterns were used in both the pattern reinstatement and ISPS analyses.
Whereas reinstatement compared an individual's encoding patterns with their own recall patterns, ISPS compared those encoding patterns with the encoding patterns of other participants (see below).

Neural patterns for each event during encoding were correlated with neural patterns for each event during spoken recall using Pearson's r across vertices, separately for each hemisphere, and Fisher z-transformed to stabilize variance.

To account for general neural similarity unrelated to event-specific reinstatement, we used the mean pattern similarity between mismatched encoding-to-recall event pairs (e.g., encoding of event A to recall of event B) as a baseline and subtracted this value from the mean pattern similarity for matched event pairs (e.g., encoding of event A to recall of event A).
Baseline-corrected reinstatement values were averaged across hemispheres, yielding one reinstatement value per participant, with higher values reflecting stronger event-specific neural reinstatement.

Using the same event-averaged encoding patterns described above, we correlated each participant's pattern for a given event with the average pattern of the remaining participants in the same age group for the corresponding event using a leave-oneout approach (within-group), or with the average pattern of the participants in the other age group (cross-group), using Pearson's r.

Resulting correlation coefficients were Fisher z-transformed and baseline-corrected by subtracting the similarity between mismatched event pairs (e.g., a participant's pattern for event A and the group-averaged pattern for event B) from the similarity for matched event pairs.

Values were averaged across events and hemispheres, yielding one within-group and one cross-group ISPS value per participant, with higher values indicating more similar PMN patterns for the same event across individuals.
For each participant, preprocessed encoding timeseries were averaged across PMN vertices within each hemisphere.

We then correlated that participant's timeseries with the average timeseries of the remaining participants in the same age group using a leave-one-out approach (within-group), or with the average timeseries of the participants in the other age group (cross-group), computing Pearson's r.
Resulting correlation coefficients were Fisher z-transformed to stabilize variance and averaged across hemispheres.
This procedure yielded one within-group and one cross-group ISC value per participant within the PMN, where higher values reflect stronger temporal alignment and greater shared neural synchrony.
